reference.source: Firestein & Kelley's Textbook of Rheumatology / Cassidy's Textbook of Pediatric Rheumatology
clinicalPearls: An autosomal dominant granulomatous autoinflammatory disease caused by gain-of-function mutations in NOD2 (CARD15)
The classic triad is granulomatous polyarthritis, dermatitis and uveitis, typically beginning in early childhood
The arthritis is often a boggy, exuberant tenosynovitis with characteristic cystic swelling of the wrists and ankles
The uveitis is frequently a severe, chronic, potentially sight-threatening panuveitis and is a leading cause of morbidity
The rash is an early, often subtle scaly or ichthyosiform/granulomatous eruption
Non-caseating granulomas on biopsy overlap histologically with sarcoidosis, but early onset and the familial triad distinguish Blau syndrome
The NOD2 mutations differ from those associated with Crohn disease and act by constitutive activation rather than loss of function
reference.pathophysiology: Blau syndrome is an autosomal dominant granulomatous disorder caused by gain-of-function mutations in NOD2 (also called CARD15), an intracellular pattern-recognition receptor that senses bacterial peptidoglycan fragments. The disease-causing mutations lie in the nucleotide-binding domain and render the receptor constitutively active, driving ligand-independent activation of the pro-inflammatory transcription factor NF-kB and dysregulated innate immune signalling. This sustained activation promotes formation of non-caseating epithelioid granulomas in the joints, skin and eyes. The mutations are mechanistically and topographically distinct from the Crohn-disease-associated NOD2 variants, which impair rather than enhance receptor function.
additionalDifferentials: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis and other vasculitides
Common variable immunodeficiency with granulomatous disease
additionalInvestigations: Biopsy of skin or synovium demonstrating non-caseating granulomas
Slit-lamp examination and full ophthalmological assessment for uveitis
Acute phase reactants and inflammatory markers
Serum angiotensin-converting enzyme and calcium to help distinguish sarcoidosis
Exclusion of infective granulomatous causes including mycobacterial studies
redFlags: Progressive joint deformity or contractures from uncontrolled granulomatous arthritis
Evidence of visceral or systemic granulomatous involvement beyond the classic triad
Ocular complications such as cataract, glaucoma or macular oedema
reference.prognosis: The joint and skin disease are often manageable, but the chronic uveitis is the principal threat to long-term outcome and can lead to visual loss if not aggressively monitored and treated; systemic involvement in atypical cases can broaden morbidity.
pitfalls: Diagnosing early-onset sarcoidosis without recognising the genetic Blau syndrome in a young child with the triad
Underestimating and under-monitoring the uveitis, allowing preventable visual loss
Confusing the gain-of-function Blau NOD2 mutations with the loss-of-function Crohn-associated variants
Mistaking the boggy tenosynovitis for ordinary juvenile idiopathic arthritis
management: Immunosuppression as the mainstay — corticosteroids and steroid-sparing agents such as methotrexate, escalating to biologics (anti-TNF, IL-1 or IL-6 inhibitors) for refractory disease
Aggressive, ophthalmology-led treatment of the sight-threatening panuveitis with combined local and systemic anti-inflammatory therapy
Regular slit-lamp surveillance to detect and control uveitis before irreversible visual loss occurs
Manage the granulomatous arthritis and tenosynovitis with anti-inflammatory therapy and physiotherapy to preserve joint function
Coordinate care across clinical immunology or rheumatology and ophthalmology
Provide genetic counselling and family assessment given autosomal dominant NOD2 inheritance
